# What's special about time {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Order is information

Tabular rows are exchangeable; time-series observations are **not**. Order creates:

- **Trend** — long-run direction
- **Seasonality** — repeating cycles (daily, weekly, annual)
- **Autocorrelation** — today resembles yesterday

And practical headaches: gaps, irregular sampling, time zones, and the choice that changes everything — **resolution**.

## Resolution changes the story

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
co2 = sm.datasets.co2.load_pandas().data.dropna()
weekly = co2["co2"]
monthly = weekly.resample("MS").mean().dropna()
yearly = weekly.resample("YS").mean()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6), sharey=True)
weekly.loc["1990":"1995"].plot(ax=axes[0], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[0].set_title("Weekly, 1990–95: the seasonal sawtooth dominates")
yearly.plot(ax=axes[1], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[1].set_title("Yearly means: only the trend survives")
for a in axes: a.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Neither is wrong. **The resolution is an editorial choice — make it consciously, state it on the chart.**

## Autocorrelation, made visible {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 2.9))
plot_acf(monthly, lags=36, ax=axes[0], title="")
axes[0].set_title("Raw series: trend dominates — everything correlates", fontsize=9.5)
plot_acf(monthly.diff().dropna(), lags=36, ax=axes[1], title="")
axes[1].set_title("After differencing: a clean spike at lag 12", fontsize=9.5)
for a in axes: a.set_xlabel("lag (months)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The **ACF** plots correlation of the series with itself at each lag. Left: slow decay is the signature of a **trend** — every month resembles the last simply because the whole thing is rising. Right: remove the trend by differencing and the **seasonality** appears as a spike at lag 12, with echoes at 24 and 36.

::: {.gw-box}
"Today resembles yesterday" is not a vibe — it is a measurable quantity with its own standard plot.
:::

# Trend & seasonality {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Smoothing reveals trend

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
monthly = co2["co2"].resample("MS").mean().dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
monthly.plot(ax=ax, alpha=0.35, label="monthly")
monthly.rolling(12).mean().plot(ax=ax, linewidth=2, label="12-month rolling mean")
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("A 12-month window averages out exactly one seasonal cycle")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Window length is a tuning knob. Matching the window to the **seasonal period** is the principled default — but see what the knob actually does.

## The window *is* the analysis {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg4 = monthly.loc["1980":"1998"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.8, 2.9))
seg4.plot(ax=axes[0], color="#bbbbbb", lw=0.9, label="monthly")
for w, c in [(3, "#d9534f"), (12, "#2E6E8E"), (60, "#6aa84f")]:
    seg4.rolling(w).mean().plot(ax=axes[0], lw=1.8, color=c, label=f"{w}-month")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=6.5); axes[0].set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
axes[0].set_title("Rolling mean: 3 keeps the season, 12 removes it, 60 flattens", fontsize=9)

seg4.rolling(12).std().plot(ax=axes[1], color="#b07aa1", lw=1.8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("ppm"); axes[1].set_xlabel("")
axes[1].set_title("Rolling std: the *amplitude* of the seasonal swing", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

- **3 months** — shorter than the cycle, so the sawtooth survives: you are smoothing noise, not seasonality
- **12 months** — exactly one cycle, so seasonality cancels and trend remains
- **60 months** — erases real turning points along with the noise

The window is not a cosmetic setting. **Rolling any statistic works** — the right panel rolls the *standard deviation*, turning "how big is the seasonal swing" into its own readable series.

## Decomposition: three series hiding in one

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose
res = seasonal_decompose(monthly, period=12)
fig = res.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8.5, 5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Trend + seasonal + residual. The **residual panel is the diagnostic**: structure left there means the model missed something. So let's put that to work.

## Additive or multiplicative? Ask the residuals {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
rng4 = np.random.default_rng(11)
n4 = 132
idx = pd.date_range("2008-01-01", periods=n4, freq="MS")
level = np.linspace(100, 320, n4)
# Swing AND noise both scale with the level — the multiplicative signature.
series = pd.Series(level * (1 + 0.16 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * np.arange(n4) / 12))
                   * (1 + rng4.normal(0, 0.012, n4)), index=idx)

add = seasonal_decompose(series, period=12, model="additive")
mul = seasonal_decompose(series, period=12, model="multiplicative")

# NB: plot through matplotlib, not Series.plot() — pandas installs its own date
# converter, which silently ignores the mdates locator and blanks the labels.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.2, 2.7))
axes[0].plot(series.index, series.values, color="#2E6E8E", lw=1.3)
axes[0].set_title("Swing grows with the level", fontsize=9)
axes[1].plot(add.resid.index, add.resid.values, color="#d9534f", lw=1.0)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
axes[1].set_title("Additive residual: big at both ends", fontsize=9)
axes[2].plot(mul.resid.index, mul.resid.values, color="#6aa84f", lw=1.0)
axes[2].axhline(1, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
axes[2].set_title("Multiplicative residual: no pattern", fontsize=9)
for a in axes:
    a.set_xlabel("")
    a.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator(3))
    a.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Additive** assumes a seasonal swing of constant size (`trend + seasonal + resid`). **Multiplicative** assumes it scales with the level (`trend × seasonal × resid`) — the usual case for anything growing, like sales or traffic.

Fitting additive here estimates **one averaged swing**, which is too big early and too small late. So the residual is large at both ends and near zero in the middle — the single point where the average happens to fit.

::: {.gw-box}
You don't guess the model: you fit one and **read the residual panel**. Leftover shape means wrong model. CO₂ is genuinely additive; most business series are not.
:::

# Uncertainty {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## A single line is a confident lie

Real series are measured with error, smoothed with choices, and forecast with doubt. Showing only the line hides all three.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
roll = monthly.rolling(12)
mean, std = roll.mean(), roll.std()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
mean.plot(ax=ax, label="12-mo mean", color="#2E6E8E")
ax.fill_between(mean.index, mean - 2*std, mean + 2*std, alpha=0.2, color="#2E6E8E", label="±2σ band")
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("The band says: values routinely range this far around the smooth line")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Bands, error bars, and intervals return in Week 13 — visualizing **model** uncertainty uses the same vocabulary.

# Time without a time axis {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Animation maps time to *time* {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
import plotly.express as px
gap = px.data.gapminder()
figa = px.scatter(gap, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", size="pop", color="continent",
                  hover_name="country", animation_frame="year", log_x=True,
                  size_max=42, range_y=[25, 90], height=350, width=1080,
                  labels={"gdpPercap": "GDP per capita", "lifeExp": "life expectancy"})
figa.update_layout(margin=dict(l=4, r=4, t=6, b=0), legend=dict(font=dict(size=10)))
figa
```

Press play. Every other chart today spent an **axis** on time; this one spends the *frames*, freeing both axes for other variables. Five variables, no time axis.

## What animation gives and takes {.smaller}

**Gains** — immediacy and narrative: the 1960→2007 sweep is felt, not read. Motion is preattentive (Week 2), so the eye is pulled to whatever moves most.

**Loses** — **persistence**. A static chart lets the reader compare any two moments at will; animation shows one frame and asks them to *remember* the rest. Precise comparison across time becomes impossible without scrubbing back.

::: {.gw-box}
Rule of thumb: animate to **engage**, small-multiple or overlay to **compare**. If the question is "how much did X change between two dates", a static chart answers it and an animation does not.
:::

# Honesty on the time axis {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The truncated-axis trick

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg = monthly.loc["1984":"1989"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
seg.plot(ax=axes[0], color="#d9534f")
axes[0].set_ylim(seg.min()-0.5, seg.max()+0.5)
axes[0].set_title("Truncated axis: 'CO₂ EXPLODES!'")
seg.plot(ax=axes[1], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[1].set_ylim(0, seg.max()*1.1)
axes[1].set_title("Zero baseline: steady ~1.5 ppm/yr rise")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same data. Truncation isn't always wrong (small real changes can matter!) — but it must be **visible and stated**, never silent.

## The aspect-ratio trick {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
seg5 = yearly.loc["1965":"2000"]
yrs = seg5.index.year          # integers, so a tick locator actually applies
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 2.8), sharey=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 2.2, 5]})
for a, t in zip(axes, ["tall & narrow:\n'runaway'", "banked near 45°:\nreadable",
                       "wide & flat:\n'nothing happening'"]):
    a.plot(yrs, seg5.values, color="#2E6E8E", lw=1.8)
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=8.5); a.set_xlabel("")
    a.xaxis.set_major_locator(plt.MaxNLocator(3, integer=True))
    a.tick_params(labelsize=6.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Identical data, identical axes, identical y-range. **Only the width changed** — and with it the perceived rate of change.

::: {.gw-box}
Cleveland's **banking to 45°**: slopes are judged most accurately when the average line segment sits near 45°. Squash or stretch away from that and you are editorializing with the figure size.
:::

## The honesty checklist for temporal charts {.smaller}

- Y-axis: zero-based, or truncation **flagged**
- Resolution: stated, chosen for the question
- Smoothing: window disclosed
- Aspect ratio: not stretched to dramatize slope
- Dual axes: almost never — they manufacture correlation

::: {.gw-box}
Week 14 returns to ethics in full; the time axis is where most everyday chart crimes happen.
:::
